questions.question: What is considered the most significant inflammatory mediator in the pathophysiology of anemia of chronic disease (AOCD)?

explanation.text: Interleukin-6 is the most important inflammatory mediator linked to the pathogenesis of anemia of chronic disease (AOCD). In chronic conditions, Interleukin-6 will increase and act on the liver. Releases Hepcidin (master regulator) Inhibits Fe absorption. Serum iron levels and transferrin saturation are decreased. Inhibits the release of Fe from ferritin. Therefore, ferritin levels increase.

This leads to a decrease in TIBC. Feature AOCD Iron Deficiency Anemia Serum iron Low Low Transferrin saturation Low Low Ferritin More Low TIBC Low More (Mnemonic: TIBC) T: Top in I: IDA B: Bottom in C: Chronic disease Interleukin-10 (Option C) is an anti-inflammatory cytokine, which supports erythropoiesis and maintains iron homeostasis. It reduces the impact of chronic inflammation on RBC production.
**Interferon-γ (Option D):** is produced by activated Th1 cells. It promotes the immune-mediated destruction of stem cells and leads to bone marrow failure and pancytopenia in aplastic anemia.

questions.question: A 65-year-old female with a history of breast cancer presents with fatigue and pallor. Laboratory results indicate a hemoglobin level of 9.7 g/dL, low serum iron, elevated ferritin, and low total iron-binding capacity (TIBC). All of the following are true regarding this condition except? Anemia is caused by reduced erythroid progenitor proliferation and iron uptake. Causes include chronic infections, autoimmune disorders and lymphoma. Peripheral smear does not show microcytic hypochromic anemia. All the patients benefit from erythropoietin administration.

explanation.text: Anemia of chronic disease Caused by reduced erythroid progenitors and impaired iron utilization (statement 1).

Common cause of anemia due to chronic diseases (statement 2), including Microbial infections: Osteomyelitis, bacterial endocarditis, lung abscess Immune disorders: Rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease Neoplasms: Lung, breast, and Hodgkin lymphoma Blood smear: Normocytic and normochromic (mostly), or hypochromic and microcytic (like IDA) (statement 3).
Management: Treat the underlying condition; some benefit with erythropoietin administration (statement 4).

questions.question: Which of the following investigations is the least helpful in determining the underlying cause of anemia?

explanation.text: The least useful investigation in determining the underlying cause of anemia is MCH (Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin). MCH measures the average amount of hemoglobin per red blood cell.

MCH can be valuable when used together with MCV to refine the classification of anemia but it does not independently yield as much diagnostic information regarding the underlying causes of anemia as other tests MCV (Option A) categorizes anemia by measuring the red blood cell size: microcytic (<80 fL), normocytic (80-100 fL), and macrocytic (>100 fL), aiding in identifying underlying causes such as iron deficiency or vitamin B12 deficiency.

Peripheral smear ( Option C) is used to assess the morphology of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, crucial in identifying abnormalities such as hypochromia, microcytosis, or macrocytosis,. Reticulocyte count ( Option D) measures the percentage of reticulocytes in the blood and can indicate the bone marrow's response to anemia.
It helps differentiate between causes of anemia related to decreased production or increased destruction or loss of red blood cells.

questions.question: A 24-year-old female with severe anemia started on parenteral iron. Which of the following would occur first in this patient as a response to therapy?

explanation.text: One of the earliest responses to the correction of iron deficiency anemia is increase in serum iron.

Responses after initiation of treatment: 12 to 24 hours Replenishment of intracellular iron enzymes, decreased irritability; increased appetite, increase in serum iron. 36 to 48 hours Erythroid hyperplasia in bone marrow 48 to 72 hours Reticulocytosis, peaking at 5-7 days 4 to 30 days Increase in hemoglobin level, increase in ferritin, increase in MCV 1 to 3 months Repletion of stores

questions.question: A 28-year-old female presented with easy fatigability and dyspnea on exertion. She was found to have a hemoglobin of 6 g/dL. What will be most likely finding in the peripheral blood smear of this patient?

explanation.text: Microcytosis (smaller than normal red cells) and hypochromia are classic findings in iron deficiency anemia, which is consistent with the patient's symptoms and low hemoglobin. In iron deficiency anemia (IDA), a peripheral blood smear can reveal characteristic changes. Hypochromic Red Blood Cells: The RBCs appear pale due to decreased hemoglobin content.

Microcytic Red Blood Cells: RBCs are smaller than normal due to decreased hemoglobin synthesis. Anisocytosis: There is significant variation in the size of RBCs. Poikilocytosis: RBCs may show abnormal shapes, such as pencil cells, target cells (codocytes), and occasionally, elliptocytes.
**Macrocytic red cells (Option A):** Macrocytosis typically indicates a deficiency in vitamin B12 or folate, not iron.

**Cabot rings (Option B):** Appear as thin, thread-like structures that form a loop or figure-eight shape within RBCs. It is composed of remnants of the nuclear material remnants from erythroblasts or megakaryocytes. Associated with megaloblastic anemia.
**Hypersegmented neutrophils (Option C):** These have more than 5 lobes in their nucleus. This condition is often associated with vitamin B12 deficiency or folate deficiency.

questions.question: A 32-year-old female diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia is prescribed oral iron supplements. Foods containing which of the following can she take to increase iron absorption?

explanation.text: Ascorbate (Vitamin C) enhances the absorption of non-heme iron (the type of iron found in plant-based foods and supplements) by reducing ferric iron (Fe³⁺) to the more soluble ferrous form (Fe²⁺), which is more readily absorbed in the duodenum. Factors affecting iron absorption: Enhancers Inhibitors Ascorbic acid Tannins Citric acid Carbonate Amino acid Oxalate Sugars in the diet Phosphate

questions.question: In a patient diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia, the values of all of the following increase except?

explanation.text: Transferrin saturation decreases in iron deficiency anemia. It is the serum iron to TIBC ratio and reflects the percentage of transferrin saturated with iron. In iron deficiency, less iron is available for binding to transferrin, leading to a decreased saturation.
**Total iron binding capacity (TIBC) (Option A):** is increased in iron deficiency anemia. It represents the maximum amount of iron that can be bound to transferrin.
**RBC protoporphyrin (Option B):** is a precursor to heme, and in the absence of sufficient iron, protoporphyrin accumulates.
**Transferrin receptor (TfR) (Option D):** expression on cells increases to enhance cellular uptake of iron when iron stores are low.

questions.question: A 10-year-old girl presented with fatigue and weakness. Her laboratory results show reduced hemoglobin, MCV 75 fl, MCH 22 pg and RDW 28. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The given clinical presentation and investigation points towards the diagnosis of Iron deficiency anemiaIron deficiency anemia typically presents with microcytic (low MCV) and hypochromic (low MCH) red blood cells. The elevated RDW suggests a wide variation in red blood cell sizes, which is characteristic of iron deficiency anemia.
Iron deficiency anemia can result from dietary lack, impaired absorption, increased iron requirement (e.g., during pregnancy), or chronic blood loss (e.g., gastrointestinal bleeding).

Clinical features include Koilonychia, alopecia, atrophic glossitis, and esophageal webs, pica and intestinal malabsorption, affecting overall nutritional status Megaloblastic anemia (Option B) usually presents with macrocytic anemia due to deficiencies in vitamin B12 or folate.
**Sideroblastic anemia (Option C):** can also present with microcytosis, but it is usually associated with ringed sideroblasts in the bone marrow and may show elevated iron indices.

**Thalassemia major (Option D):** usually presents in infancy or early childhood with severe anemia, failure to thrive, and a need for regular blood transfusions. This patient’s high RDW (28) suggests iron deficiency anemia, as thalassemia typically shows a normal RDW due to uniformly small red cells.There’s no mention of classic features of thalassemia major, such as hepatosplenomegaly or bone deformities. Lastly, the MCV of 75 fL is low but not as profoundly low as usually seen in thalassemia major.

questions.question: A 45-year-old male patient was diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia. Which of the following is true about the intracellular regulation of iron in the above condition? IRP- Iron regulatory protein IRE- Iron response elements

options.A: Ferritin translation is increased by binding IRP to IRE.
options.B: Ferritin translation is decreased by binding IRP to IRE.
options.C: Transferrin receptor 1 translation is unaffected by binding IRP to IRE.
options.D: Transferrin receptor 1 translation is decreased by binding IRP to IRE.

explanation.text: In iron deficiency anemia, ferritin translation is decreased by binding iron regulatory protein to iron response elements. Iron regulatory mechanism: IRP: Binds to IREs in specific mRNAs' untranslated regions (UTRs) to control the translation of proteins involved in iron metabolism.

IRE: These are sequences found in the mRNAs of proteins involved in iron metabolism, such as ferritin and transferrin receptor 1 Ferritin: Ferritin stores iron inside cells. When iron levels are low, IRPs bind to IREs in the 5' UTR of ferritin mRNA, preventing its translation to conserve iron. Transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1): TfR1 imports iron into cells.
When iron levels are low, IRPs bind to IREs in the 3' UTR of TfR1 mRNA, stabilizing it and increasing its translation to enhance iron uptake.

questions.question: Which transport molecule facilitates the absorption of Fe2+ into enterocytes in the small intestine?

explanation.text: DMT-1 is a transmembrane protein that facilitates the transport of divalent metal ions, primarily ferrous iron (Fe 2+ ), across the apical membrane of enterocytes in the duodenum. Heme iron enters the intestinal cells directly through a heme transporter. Non-heme iron (Fe³⁺) is first reduced to Fe²⁺ by duodenal cytochrome B, then Fe²⁺ enters the cells via the DMT-1 transporter (Option C).
Inside the duodenal cell, Fe²⁺ can either be stored as mucosal iron or transported into the bloodstream.
**Fe²⁺ exits the cell through ferroportin (Option A):** .

**In the blood, Fe²⁺ is oxidized to Fe³⁺ by hephaestin (Option B):** and ceruloplasmin. Fe³⁺ binds to transferrin for delivery to the bone marrow, where it is stored as ferritin; in cases of hemolysis, ferritin aggregates to form hemosiderin.
**The liver secretes hepcidin (Option D):** , a protein that regulates iron absorption. When iron stores are adequate, hepcidin downregulates ferroportin expression, reducing iron absorption.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with fatigue and pallor. Lab tests show hemoglobin of 9 g/dL and MCV of 68 fL. Peripheral smear reveals microcytic and hypochromic red blood cells. Her symptoms and laboratory findings are consistent with iron deficiency anemia. Which of the following statements regarding iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is correct?

options.B: Serum ferritin is the gold standard investigation
options.D: Serum ferritin levels are not affected.

explanation.text: Serum ferritin is a key marker used in diagnosing iron deficiency anemia. In iron deficiency, ferritin levels are decreased because ferritin stores decrease as iron stores deplete. (Option A and D) Serum ferritin levels below 30 ng/mL are generally considered indicative of depleted iron stores and are a reliable marker for iron deficiency.

**Serum ferritin is the gold standard investigation (Option B):** While serum ferritin is commonly used as a marker for iron stores, it is not considered the gold standard test for diagnosing iron deficiency. A bone marrow aspirate to directly assess iron stores is the gold standard for diagnosing iron deficiency.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman has been experiencing fatigue, pallor, and shortness of breath for the past six months. Laboratory tests reveal a Hb of 6 gm/dl. Red cell distribution width is increased. Peripheral smear is shown below. Where is the likely site of absorption of the micronutrient deficient in this patient?

explanation.text: The given clinical presentation of low hemoglobin, increased RDW, and microcytic hypochromic red cells on peripheral smear, points towards the diagnosis of Iron deficiency anemia. Iron is primarily absorbed through the duodenal mucosa, making duodenum the most likely site of absorption. Metabolism of iron: Iron from the diet (heme and non-heme) is converted to ferrous form in the stomach.

Heme iron is primarily found in animal-based foods, while non heme iron is found in plant-based foods and iron-fortified foods. In the duodenum, ferrous iron is absorbed via DMT1 and transported into enterocytes. Inside, it binds to ferritin or enters the bloodstream via ferroportin. Iron binds to transferrin in the blood, facilitating its delivery to tissues for functions like hemoglobin synthesis.
Hepcidin, a peptide hormone produced by the liver, plays a crucial role in regulating iron homeostasis.
**Jejunum (Option A):** absorbs nutrients like amino acids, glucose, fatty acids, and folic acid.
**Ileum (Option B):** completes nutrient absorption, including bile salts, vitamin B12, and remaining nutrients, before the material enters the colon.
**Colon (Option D):** focuses on absorbing water, electrolytes like sodium and chloride, and some vitamins from gut bacteria, such as vitamin K and biotin.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the normal metabolism of vitamin B12? A. Haptocorrin from salivary glands binds to B12 in the stomach. B. It is absorbed in the duodenum with the help of intrinsic factor and transcobalamin II. C. Gastric enzymes play an important role in splitting of haptocorrin-B12 complex. D. It is stored primarily in the liver and has a large reserve capacity. E. It acts as a cofactor for converting homocysteine to methionine and methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA.

explanation.text: Vitamin B12 Absorption and Transport: Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum (Option B).
**Haptocorrin, secreted by the salivary gland, binds to B12 in the stomach and enters the duodenum (Option A):** .
**Haptocorrin is separated from B12 by pancreatic enzymes and binds to IF (Option C):** .
**Absorbed B12 is transported by transcobalamin II (Option B):** .

**Stored primarily in the liver and has a large reserve capacity to last several years (Option D):** . Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for: (Option E) Conversion of homocysteine to methionine. Methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA.

explanation.text: Chronic alcoholism causes megaloblastic anaemia due to folate deficiency. Causes of Vitamin B12 deficiency: Reduced Dietary Intake Increased demand Impaired Absorption Vegetarian diet Pregnancy Lactation Growing child Pernicious anemia (Option A) Infections- Diphyllobothrium latum (Option C) Gastrectomy (Option:D) Ileal disorders Malabsorption Ileal resection Diverticula of bowel

questions.question: A 60-year-old female presents with chronic fatigue, shortness of breath, tingling and numbness in her hands and feet, bloating, and epigastric pain after meals. She has a history of occasional heartburn and nausea. On examination, she is pale, has a smooth, enlarged tongue with the following findings on the hand. Lab investigations show haemoglobin to be 9.6 g% and MCV 112. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: Pernicious anaemia is the likely diagnosis due to macrocytic anaemia (high MCV), chronic fatigue, neurological symptoms (tingling and numbness), and gastrointestinal issues (bloating and epigastric pain). The physical signs of pallor and a smooth, enlarged tongue, along with the image of knuckle hyperpigmentation further indicate vitamin B12 deficiency, characteristic of pernicious anaemia.

Pernicious Anemia: Pernicious anaemia is a specific form of megaloblastic anaemia caused by autoimmune gastritis that impairs the production of the intrinsic factor required for vitamin B12 uptake from the gut. Three types of antibodies: Type 1: Inhibit B12 binding to intrinsic factor. Type 2: Inhibit B12-IF binding to iliac cubilin receptors. Type 3: Target parietal cells. Clinical features: Fatigue and pallor.

Hyperpigmentation: Mainly on knuckles and interphalangeal areas. Atrophic glossitis (beefy red smooth tongue). Atrophic gastritis (due to antibodies against parietal cells). Increased gastric adenocarcinoma risk. Neurological manifestations: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal tract. Both sensory and motor loss (combined degeneration) Headache, fatigue, impaired balance, paresthesia, muscle weakness and neuropathy.

Blood smear: Iron deficiency anaemia typically presents with microcytic anaemia (Option A). Folate deficiency can present with macrocytic anaemia but is less likely to cause neurological symptoms and knuckle hyperpigmentation (Option B). Thalassemia presents with microcytic anaemia and is not associated with hyperpigmentation or neurological symptoms (Option C).

questions.question: Match the following laboratory findings with the most likely diagnosis. a. Microcytic anaemia, normal homocysteine and methylmalonic acid levels. 1. Vitamin B12 Deficiency b. Anaemia of Chronic Disease (ACD) d. Normocytic anaemia, normal homocysteine and methylmalonic acid levels. 4. Folate Deficiency

explanation.text: Disease Lab Findings Blood Smear Vitamin B12 Deficiency RBC Indices: Hemoglobin(Hb): low. MCV: high (> 100fL). MCH: high. MCHC: normal. Homocysteine: Low Methylmalonic acid: Low. Macrocytic hyperchromic anemia. Folate Deficiency RBC Indices: Hemoglobin(Hb): low. MCV: high (> 100fL). MCH: high. MCHC: normal. Homocysteine: Low Methylmalonic acid: Normal.

Iron deficiency anaemia & anaemia of chronic disease (AOCD): Microcytic hypochromic anaemia is seen (AOCD: Normocytic normochromic > microcytic hypochromic). Homocysteine & methylmalonic acid levels are normal.

questions.question: All the following findings are seen in vitamin B12 deficiency except?

options.B: Sieve-like chromatin on bone marrow smear

explanation.text: The normal myeloid: erythroid ratio is 3:1. In vitamin B12 deficiency, a reversal of myeloid: erythroid ratio is seen (1:3). Important Laboratory findings associated with Vitamin B12 deficiency: Bone Marrow Biochemical Tests Hypercellular bone marrow Erythroid Hyperplasia Sieve-like chromatin (Option: B).

Hypersegmented neutrophils Reversal of myeloid: erythroid ratio 1:1 or less (Normal: 3:1) (Option A) Nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony Serum bilirubin: Increases (Option: D). Serum LDH: Increases (Option: C). Vitamin B12: Decreases Folic acid: Decreases Anti-Intrinsic Factor (IF) antibody: Present (Pernicious anemia) Methylmalonyl CoA: Increases Homocysteine: Increases Schilling Test: Assess cause of B12 deficiency.

questions.question: A patient presents with tiredness and myalgia for the past 3 months. She has hypertension, psoriasis and hyperuricemia, for which she is on multiple medications. A peripheral blood smear is done which is given in the image below. Which of her following medications would have caused these symptoms?

explanation.text: The peripheral blood smear shows enlarged oval-shaped red blood cells (macro-ovalocytes) with hyperchromia and hypersegmented neutrophils. This suggests megaloblastic anaemia, which in this scenario would be due to folate deficiency caused by methotrexate. Common causes of folate deficiency are given below: Decreased intake Inadequate diet. Alcoholism. Infancy. Impaired absorption Malabsorption states. Intrinsic intestinal disease.

Anticonvulsants, oral contraceptives. Increased loss Haemodialysis. Increased requirement Pregnancy. Infancy. Disseminated cancer. Markedly increased hematopoiesis. Impaired utilisation Folic acid antagonists (Methotrexate).
